results.title: How should Feature Selection and Hyperparameter optimization be ordered in the machine learning pipeline? - Cross Validated
results.content: In ii) and iii), there are hyperparameters like k-Nearest Neigbours for ReliefF or the window length, for which the sensor signal is evaluated, or the number of hidden units in each layer of N.N. There are 3 Problems I see here : 1) Tuning feature selection parameters will influence the classifier performance 2) Optimizing hyperparameters of classifier will influence the choice of features. To address the additional question that Nikolas posted in the comments, concering how all these things (feature selection, hyperparameter optimization) interact with k-fold cross validation: I'd say it depends. 1. Repeat the complete pipeline within every fold separately (e.g. within each fold, do feature selection + hyperparameter optimization and training model). Then, you fix your selected features and hyperparameters, and do k-fold cross validation on the ''train/test dataset''. Doing this means that k-fold cross validation gives you **unbiased estimates of the performance of your ML algorithm given the fixed feature-set and hyperparameter values**. If you're, for example, a company that intends to have the complete pipeline of feature selection + hyperparameter optimization + training running automatically every day/week/month/year/whatever, you'll also be interested in the performance of that complete pipeline, and you'll want the first solution. If, on the other hand, you can only afford to do the feature selection + hyperparameter optimization a single time in your life, and afterwards only somewhat regularly re-train your algorithm (with feature-set and hyperparam values fixed), then the performance of only that step will be what you're interested in, and you should go for the second solution. For feature selection, we can run whatever method on the training data and get a feature set, but for hyperparameter tuning, don't we need to cross validate on the training data again? -> Perform nested cross validation with the initial features and the hyperparameter_train set to find the best hyperparameters as outlined in option 1. -> Use the best hyperparameters and the feature_selection_train set to find the best set of features. results.title: What are the best Practices When Doing Hyperparameter Tuning?
results.content: Essentially, when a model of data scientists doesn't work as expected, they search for this sort of harmonization (Fine-Tuning Process). 🥼 In my experience with data science, random searches, grid searches, and cross-validation procedures have been demonstrated to be the most successful methods of fine-tuning hyperparameters when I was a new bee and had very little experience with them at the time. 1️⃣ Manual Search: Straightforward hyperparameter-tuning method. 2️⃣ Grid Search: simplest automated hyperparameter-tuning method such as for loop approach the evaluating the best parameters. 3️⃣ Random Search: Simplest hyperparameter tuning method works best in all three, surprisingly. Pros: categorize features well, big search space, handle conditional hyperparameters. Pros: Big Search Space; handles all types of hyperparameters; conditional hyperparameters;. Cons: work on numerical hyperparameters, not use for big hyperparameter space, Can't exploit the parallel computing. This method is similar to the random search hyperparameter tuning method. Pros: Similar to random search, focus on search space that gives better optimal parameters. Cons: Similar to random search, skip some parts of search space where chances of best hyperparameters, High Computation cost. Pros: Support Parallel Computing, Exploitation is based on multiple candidates, works for both types of hyperparameters. Cons: Not support expensive objective function, High Computation cost same as GAs, work well with continues hyperparameters. Pros: Act only as hyperparameter tuning but also support model training, Support parallel Computing, Exploitation is done based on multiple candidates. Cons: Work only with Neural network-based models, High Computations like GAs. MFO is a group of hyperparameter tuning methods that work by creating a cheap approximation of the whole hyperparameter tuning pipeline so that we can get similar performance results with much lower computational cost and faster experiment time. 2️⃣ Successive Halving: It is an MFO method that is not only able to focus on a more promising hyperparameter subspace but can also allocate computational cost wisely in each trial. 4️⃣ BOHB: BOHB (Bayesian Optimization and Hyperband) performs robust and efficient hyperparameter optimization at scale by combining the speed of hyperband searches with the guidance and guarantees of convergence of Bayesian Optimization.

results.title: matlab - What is the proper way to implement a real time spectrogram? - Signal Processing Stack Exchange
results.content: # What is the proper way to implement a real time spectrogram? I am trying to implement a real time spectrogram and I am not sure that I am implementing it the right way. not so sure how **short** the snippets of audio are in a commercial real-time analyzer, but you should know that the **frameLength** (which is also the window width) and the **frameHop** are two different numbers if there is anything better than 0% overlap. Spectrograms are normally computed using the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), and can be done in real-time. If you want more frequency resolution, you can use longer FFTs. In order to update with low latency (closer to "real time"), you can input short buffers often (every few milliseconds). * $\begingroup$ This is not how I understood the overlap approach: the overlap and add is done on the FFT result so does not result in a longer FFT but avoids the amplitude loss we would have over intervals in the time domain if the data was not overlapped. * $\begingroup$ Right - that is how I understood it for creating a spectrogram (such as explained here:tek.com/en/documents/primer/…) : each FFT is the length of the buffer, rather than overlapping the data in time to then FFT an effectively longer buffer as your answer is written; that wording confused me. Although you can use the STFT to calculate a spectrogram, you will have a time-frequency trade-off. Second, you need to decide your STFT properties (especially the overlap percent) so you can match your computation time with your target real-time update, $\Delta t$. The least possible computation time is when you have an overlap of $0$ or hop size is $L$ ($L$ is the window size), meaning every sampling time, $T\_s$, you will update your STFT property. In my spectrogram below, done in python, I use an overlap of $50\%$ (which is the usual percent) so I have a waiting time more than $T\_s$ to compute and update my STFT. $\begingroup$ Didn't you mean "hop size" instead of "overlap" in "least possible computation time is when you have an overlap of $L−1$"?

results.content: We have zero knowledge about time in Fourier transform.Now comes the next question if we dont know exact time at which frequency is taken from the audio ,then how  Fourier transform giving an output like below. So the answer is Fourier transform is taken for the whole audio .Note that the frequency amplitude diagram generated by the FT does not consider time explicitly. "The STFT computes the Fourier" Transform on small, overlapping time windows of the signal, allowing us to observe the frequency content at different points in time.This enables us  to capture frequency over time information which was lacking in Fourier Transform.In other words, the STFT provides a time-frequency representation of the signal**.**The diagram below shows an example of how STFT looks like.And visualisation of STFT is called Spectrogram. This blog has explored fundamental methods in audio signal processing—specifically, Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) and Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC). We've seen how STFT breaks down audio into manageable segments to capture time-frequency information, contrasting with the holistic view provided by Fourier Transform.
